articles.title: Wildlife populations have declined 73% since 1970—but many of the world's animals still aren't being counted
articles.source: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
articles.summary: Wildlife populations around the world have declined by an average of 73% since 1970. That's according to the WWF's new 2026 Living Planet Index—a major estimate, updated every two years, of the changing state of nature. This does not mean that 73% of the world's animals have disappeared. Rather, it is the average decline in the size of wildlife populations being monitored.

articles.title: 'DNA Typewriter' records cells' history in developing mouse embryo
articles.source: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
articles.summary: Scientists have succeeded in reconstructing the family tree of cells in a developing mouse embryo. They recorded cells' relationships, starting when the fertilized egg first split in two and ending after the body and its organs took shape. That period lasted 13.5 days. (Full gestation in mice is 19 to 21 days.)

articles.title: Quantum 'birthmarks' hold lasting traces of a system's past
articles.source: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
articles.summary: Some classical physical systems can explore many configurations over time until their long-term behavior no longer reveals their starting conditions. The sampling of available configurations according to the appropriate statistical distribution is a property called ergodicity.

articles.title: Scientists build a nuclear clock that could make atomic clocks obsolete
articles.summary: Scientists in Vienna have achieved a major breakthrough in timekeeping by creating the world’s first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, a technology that could eventually surpass even the most precise atomic clocks. Instead of relying on electrons in atoms, the clock uses the tiny nuclei of thorium atoms, which are far less sensitive to outside disturbances.
